articles.text: The Mandan Pioneer, to further its scheme of division on the Missouri river, states in a recent article that the cattlemen are anxious to have the Territory divided and want it divided on the river. We have been at considerable pains to learn the sentiment among stockmen and find that the opposite opinion is almost unanimous. As business men, they look at the proposition from a business point of view and can scarcely see the object of doubling expenses without a corresponding benefit. In this case, there is absolutely no benefit whatever to be gained, but in case the western part should be admitted, the expense of running a state government would be more than double what it would be if the Territory were admitted as a whole. This is not only the sentiment of the people here, but that of nine-tenths of the people of all Dakota, "Admission without division." It can be put down as an axiom that every man or paper crying for division has an axe to grind. Of course it is manifest that in case this division is made, the Pioneer expects Mandan to become the capital of western Dakota. In this, it is greatly mistaken. The capital location, as here-to-fore, will be a matter of bargain and sale. In that event, there will be other towns, for instance the terminus of a railroad in the Black Hills, which can easily put up ten dollars to Mandan's one. In any event, western Dakota is not and for many years will not be able to support a state government. And now, will the Pioneer or any other axe-grinding division paper tell us a few good reasons why Dakota should be divided at all? Why not make it one magnificent state that will stand among the first of her sister states, instead of two states, neither of which can expect to occupy higher than a middle position?
articles.summary: Editorial rejecting the Mandan Pioneer's claim that cattlemen want Dakota divided on the Missouri river, arguing for "Admission without division."

articles.headline: STRAYED.
articles.text:
STOCK NOTES.

STRAYED.

About April 15th., a bay gelding four years old, branded [brand] on left shoulder and VI on left hip. Had hackamore on when lost. Finder please notify,

Howard Eaton or Cow Boy office, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton's notice of a bay gelding (VI on left hip) strayed about April 15.

articles.headline: STRAYED.
articles.text:
One bay horse weight about 900 pounds with small white spot in forehead branded C— on left thigh, had on when last seen, a hackamore with a rope dragging. A suitable reward will be paid for the return of the horse to my ranch, information where he can be found. Ranch six miles north of track on Beaver.

S. E. Grindall, Mingusville, Montana.
articles.summary: S. E. Grindall of Mingusville offers a reward for a strayed bay horse.

articles.headline: For Sale.
articles.text:
I have now on the trail 4,500 head of improved Texas cattle, yearlings and two-year-olds mostly steers. They will be in the Bad Lands about August 25. Thirteen hundred head of these cattle are for sale. Address all communications to

B. F. Reynolds, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: B. F. Reynolds announces 4,500 Texas cattle on the trail, due in the Bad Lands about August 25, 1,300 of them for sale.

articles.headline: STRAYED.
articles.text:
From the VI ranch on or about July 4, three sorrel horses branded VI on left hip. When last seen were near the "Capital B" ranch. Any information leading to the recovery of the horses may be sent to the Cow Boy office, to the Stockgrowers' Journal of Miles City, or to

Howard Eaton, Medora, Dak.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton seeks three sorrel VI horses strayed from the VI ranch about July 4.

articles.text: T. Brickley and A. Haxby, of the FOX outfit, recently located on Crooked creek, were in Medora Tuesday and made the Cow Boy a visit.
articles.summary: Brickley and Haxby of the FOX outfit on Crooked creek visit Medora.

articles.text: The first shipment of cattle over the Northern Pacific to the Chicago market took place Aug. 1. The shipment was from Miles City and took twenty cars.
articles.summary: First Northern Pacific cattle shipment of the season to Chicago left Miles City Aug. 1.

articles.text: Harry Tarbell has had printed a supply of postal cards giving notice, that two geldings and five mares strayed or were stolen from the Little Missouri Horse Co.'s ranch on Deep creek. They were branded TW connected on either shoulder or JS on right hip or left shoulder, one or both brands being used.
articles.summary: Harry Tarbell circulates postal cards about seven horses strayed or stolen from the Little Missouri Horse Co. ranch on Deep creek.

articles.text: Hecht, Freeze & Young of Rapid City, have brought about 1,200 stock cattle from their Cheyenne river range to Crooked creek on the stage route. Their brand is Z on shoulder and TS connected on side. Mr. M. Kelliher, of Rapid City, has also brought about 1,200 stock cattle to the same range. His brand is FOX on side and LK connected on thigh. This range is one of the best in the country and we expect to hear good results from the cattle. The headquarters of the two outfits will probably be in Medora.
articles.summary: Two Rapid City outfits bring about 2,400 stock cattle to Crooked creek, with headquarters probably in Medora.

articles.headline: Cow Boy Dictionary.
articles.text:
A revision of Webster's dictionary is now being made and will be published some time during the year. In looking through the pages of a late edition, we found scarcely one of the words referring to the cattle business and in common use here. We wrote to this effect to the revisers and received a pressing invitation to gather together a complete collection of cowboy and other western words to be published in the next issue of the dictionary. We do not claim perfection in any way for the following list. We publish it for the purpose of having additions and corrections made. A few words have been left out because their proper definition is already given, but it by no means indicates that if a word is lacking that we do not want it. The very commonest words are the ones most likely to be missed altogether. If a number of persons will send us in additions and corrections we can be moderately sure of a full list. Our list extends through the "O's" this issue and will be concluded in our next.

A

Aparejos, n. (Definition wanted.)

B

Brand, n. (cattle.) A mark burned or cut on an animal, signifying ownership.

Brand, v. t. (cattle.) To burn or cut a mark on an animal.

Brand-book, n. A book containing all recorded brands of an association or district.

Branding-chute, n. A narrow enclosure, wide enough for the passage of a single animal, where it may be held convenient for branding.

Branding-iron, n. A metal device usually made of iron, which, when heated and pressed against an animal forms the brand.

Break, v. t. To accustom to the saddle or harness. To break a horse. Syn. To train.

Brow-band, n. The part of a bridle passing over the brow of a horse and holding the throat-latch and cheek-straps in place.

Buck, v. i. A violent jumping by a horse, stiff-legged, forward or side-wise up and down. Confined to western horses.

Bucker, n. A horse that bucks.

Buck-strap, n. A strap secured to the saddle to enable the rider to keep his seat on a bucking horse.

Broncho, n. (Bronko.) [Derivation unknown.] An unbroken western horse.

Bed-ground, n. The place used to hold cattle at night.

Bridle-wise, adj. Referring to a quality of being guided by a bridle.

Buffalo-trail, n. A path worn by buffaloes.

Buffalo-wallow, n. A bowl shaped hole worn into the ground by buffaloes while rolling.

Buffalo-berry, n. A berry growing on bushes, something like the whortleberry, peculiar to the northwest.

Bull-berry, n. See buffalo-berry.

Bull-whacker, n. A man who drives oxen.

Bunch, n. A small herd of cattle.

Bunch-grass, n. A very nutritious kind of grass, about six inches high, growing on western prairies. It is the principal feed for stock in the west.

Buzzard-head, n. A lazy or useless horse.

C

Cabello (cavayard), n. The bunch of cattle following the round-up, or belonging to private persons.

Cache (cash), v. t. To hide.

Cache (cash), n. The place where a thing is hidden.

Camp-rustler, n. A ranch cook.

Cabalo (cavi-ya), n. A horse.

California-bit, n. A spade-bit having an iron curb.

Cavejo, (Definition wanted).

Cayuse (ki-use), n. 1. Indian pony. 2. Derogatory name for a horse.

Chapparal, n. Thick under-brush.

Chapparejo, (always contractedand pronounced "shaps"). Leathern pants used by cow-boys to protect their legs from wet, cold and under-brush.

Cheek-straps, n. Straps of a bridle passing over the head of a horse down his cheeks and holding the bit in the mouth.

Chute, n. See branding-chute.

Cincha (always pronounced "sinch"), n. A strap or web belt passing under the horse's belly holdihg the saddle in place. There may be one or two cinches. An expression of superiority. "I have the cinch on him."

Close-herd, v. t. To keep a bunch of cattle together and prevent them from wandering.

Concha, n. Silver or metal ornaments in the shape of buttons worn on the outside of a spur.

Corona, n. A fancy cover for a saddle-blanket.

Corrall, n. An enclosure made of logs, rails or boards in which to keep cattle or horses.

Coulie or coulee, n. A small ravine, usually having at the bottom, the bed of a dry creek, lined with under-brush.

Counter-brand, v. t. To repeat the original brand immediately under the original.

Counter-brand, n. A repetition of the original brand on an animal, signifying that the animal is sold to some one other than the owner of the original brand.

Couresta, n. A hempen rope.

Cource, n. Leather cover for half-breed saddle.

Cow-boy, n. A person hired to take care of range cattle.

Cow-camp, n. A cattle-ranch.

Cow-girl, n. Feminine of cow-boy.

Cow-man, n. An owner of cattle.

Cow-puncher, n. See cow-boy.

Crease, v. t. To shoot a wild animal especially a horse, in the neck, over the spinal column, stunning him temporarily, for the purpose of catching him.

Cricket-bit, n. A peculiar kind of cow-boy bridle-bit having a grooved wheel, which, rolling on the horse's tongue, gives rise to the name.

Cutting-horse, n. A horse used to cut out cattle from a herd.

Cut-out, v. t. To separate from a herd a [particular?] animal or animals wanted.

Crop, v. t. To cut off the end of an animals ear. An ear-mark signifying ownership.

Crop, n. An ear-mark on an animal made by cutting the end of the ear square off.

D

Doga, n. A motherless calf.

Dewlap, n. A cut on the lower part of the neck of an animal by which a piece of skin is detached, holding by the end. It has the same significance of ownership as a brand or ear-mark.

Day-herd, n. A herd of cattle held and grazed during the day.

Double-cinch, adj. Referring to a saddle having two cinchas.

Double-rig, adj. See double-cinch.

Drags, n. The footsore and weary cattle on a drive which fall to the rear.

Draw, n. See coulie.

Dug-out, n. A kind of house built by digging into the side of a hill.

E

Ear-mark, n. A cutting or slitting of ear or ears of cattle to signify ownership.

G

Gag-bit, n. General name for all bits except snaffle and straight bits. A bit that will force the horse to open his mouth.

Grade, adj. Referring to improved cattle, viz. those having any proportion of pure blood.

Grass-cattle, n. Those living and fattening on grass alone. In general, all range cattle.

Grass-rope, n. A hempen rope.

Greaser, n. A Mexican having negro, Indian and white blood in his veins.

Grub, n. An ear-mark made by cutting the ear square off at the roots.

H

Hackamore, n. A head-gear for horses used for the same purpose as a bridle. It is usually made of horse-hair.

Half-breed-bit, n. A peculiar kind of gag-bit used by cow-boys.

Half-breed-cow, n. A cross between a Texas cow and a blooded bull.

Half-breed-horse, n. A cross between a wild mare and thoroughbred stallion.

Half-breed-saddle, n. A saddle having a Texas tree and a California rig.

Hat-string, n. Strings, usually of leather, worn by cow-boys, to keep their sombreros on.

Head, v. To ride against or in front of an animal, turning it in the direction wanted.

Heel, v. To throw the lariat in such a way as to catch the hind leg or legs of an animal to throw it down.

Horn, n. The front part of a saddle. The pommel.

Horse-wrangler, n. The man who takes care of a bunch of cow-horses in the daytime.

J

Jinglebob, n. A slitting of the ear of an animal in such a way that the end of the ear lops down. It is a mark signifying ownership.

L

Latigo-straps, n. The straps connecting the cinchas with the saddle.

Legadero, (definition wanted).

Line-riding, v. The act of riding back and forth over certain territory to keep cattle within specified limits.

Loco, n. A weed poisonous to stock.

Loco, v. To poison animals with loco weed, making them crazy.

M

Maverick, n. Any unbranded neat animal not following its mother. Term originated from a man named Maverick who turned loose a lot of unbranded cattle in Texas and then began branding everything with no brand on.

McCarty, n. A hair rope fastened to a hackamore.

Milling, v. Cattle in act of running around in a close circle.

Mule-skinner, n. A man who drives a mule team in a freight outfit.

N

Night-herd, v. To take care of animals at night.

O

Outfit, n. In cattle parlance, usually meaning; the herd, ranch &c.

Over-bit, n. A v-shaped cut in the top of the ear. An ear-mark signifying ownership.

Over-hack, n. A straight cut in the top of the ear. An ear-mark signifying ownership.

Over-half-crop, n. An ear-mark, signifying ownership, by which the outer and upper half of the ear is cut away.

Over-slope, n. An ear-mark, signifying ownership, by which the top part of the ear is cut away from the middle to the point.

(To be continued.)
articles.summary: First installment (A through O) of Packard's "Cow Boy Dictionary" of range terms, compiled for the revisers of Webster's dictionary, with a call for additions and corrections.

articles.text: Dr. Jorgens will soon return from his Cave Hills and Spearfish trip.
articles.summary: Dr. Jorgens expected back from a Cave Hills and Spearfish trip.

articles.text: Prairie chickens are unusually abundant and are already in prime condition.
articles.summary: Prairie chickens abundant and in prime condition.

articles.text: Joe Ferris' store-room is nearly completed and he will probably move in next week.
articles.summary: Joe Ferris' new store-room nearly done.

articles.text: W. G. Taffinder, Ass't. Sec. of the Insurance company of Dakota, was here Sunday and Monday.
articles.summary: Insurance company official W. G. Taffinder visits.

articles.text: A. Osborne has put in a bunch of cattle on Andrew's creek and will add to his stock next spring.
articles.summary: A. Osborne stocks cattle on Andrew's creek.

articles.text: Sheriff Harmon, of Morton county, was in Medora this morning, impanelling jurors for the district court.
articles.summary: Morton county sheriff in Medora impanelling jurors.

articles.text: The bridges on Sully creek have all or nearly all been washed out. They should be repaired immediately.
articles.summary: Sully creek bridges washed out.

articles.text: B. F. Lamb has completed a fine ranch building four miles down the river and in the spring will stock his range with a good lot of cattle.
articles.summary: B. F. Lamb completes a ranch building down the river.

articles.text: Rev. Huntley, superintendent of Dakota missions, preached here last Sunday evening. Services will be held as usual next Sunday evening.
articles.summary: Rev. Huntley preaches in Medora.

articles.text: Harry Barker takes Geo. Wilkes' place as engineer at the slaughter-house and Charles M. Tibbetts takes the positions of night engineer and watchman.
articles.summary: Staff changes at the slaughter-house.

articles.text: Geo. Wilkes severed his connection with the company last week and went to his home in Chicago. His resignation was due to a conflict of authority and reflects in no way upon his ability as an engineer, of which there is no question. His Chicago address is 190 Campbell avenue.
articles.summary: Engineer Geo. Wilkes resigns and returns to Chicago.

articles.text: A very pleasant house-warming took place in Joe Ferris' store Tuesday night. All enjoyed themselves thoroughly tripping the "light fantastic."
articles.summary: House-warming dance in Joe Ferris' store.

articles.text: The rink is being refurnished in good shape and its appearance is consequently much improved. Bob. Roberts will move in as soon as it is finished.
articles.summary: The rink is refurnished; Bob Roberts to move in.

articles.text: Between grass-hoppers and its being an off year, Montana will be short on hay this year. It is well that there is such an abudant crop in Dakota.
articles.summary: Montana short of hay; Dakota crop abundant.

articles.text: Word comes in a rather round-about way that Wilmot Dow, one of the managers of the Elkhorn ranch was married last week in Maine. We commiserate.
articles.summary: Elkhorn manager Wilmot Dow reported married in Maine.

articles.text: B. F. Reynolds and J. C. Fisher started Tuesday on a trip down the river, to or below the mouth of Beaver. Mr. Reynolds is looking up a range for his cattle.
articles.summary: Reynolds and Fisher go down the river seeking a range.

articles.text: The middle Grand stage station has been burned and others are likely to go. Mr. Paddock, on his recent trip extinguished the fire from one that was just catching.
articles.summary: Middle Grand stage station burned; Paddock puts out a fire at another.

articles.text: A hard hail-storm visited Medora last evening. If it had been accompanied by wind doubtless much loss would have resulted. As it was, the gardens probably suffered severely and a number of window lights were broken.
articles.summary: Hail-storm hits Medora.

articles.text: Five hundred Hashknife cattle were weighed out to the Co. Aug. 1. They averaged 1064½ pounds. Three of them weighed 4980 pounds and one weighed 1950 pounds. The last only dressed 1116 pounds, showing he was not in good condition.
articles.summary: Five hundred Hashknife cattle weighed out to the Co. Aug. 1.

articles.text: Last night No. 1 consisted of fourteen cars and two engines, probably the largest passenger train ever seen on the road. Several of the cars were filled with Boston excursionists and the air was positively oppressive from the vast amount of "culchah" lying around in chuncks.
articles.summary: Huge No. 1 passenger train carries Boston excursionists.

articles.text: We wish to call special attention of all to cur "cow-boy Dictionary." As stated, we do not claim perfection in any way for it. It is published principally to have corrections made to it. All should take pride in making it as complete as possible by sending or handing us corrections.
articles.summary: Packard asks readers to send corrections to the Cow Boy Dictionary.

articles.text: The two-year-old daughter of J. A. Freeze, died at about seven o'clock last evening. She will be buried at five o'clock this afternoon on the coal mine butte. Our citizens sympathize deeply with Mr. and Mrs. Freeze, as the child was a general favorite.
articles.summary: Death of J. A. Freeze's two-year-old daughter (first of two printings of the item).

articles.text: The two-year-old daughter of J. A. Freeze died at seven o'clock last evening of cholera infantum. The funeral services, led by T. W. Gordon, will take place at five o'clock, on the coal-mine butte. Our citizens sympathize deeply with Mr. and Mrs. Freeze in their loss, as the child was a general favorite.
articles.summary: Death of J. A. Freeze's daughter of cholera infantum; funeral led by T. W. Gordon (second, fuller printing of the item).

articles.text: A number of changes have been made in the running of the N. P. Ref. Car Co., chief of which are the renting of all the cold-storage houses to outside parties. The local business along the line is to be discontinued as it pays better to wholesale. The Marquis is still in the east making the necessary changes.
articles.summary: Changes at the Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co.; the Marquis is in the east.

articles.text: The two horse-thieves who have made Medora three visits and known as the "Two Jacks," have been captured at Mitchell. It will be remembered that about four months ago they were here and sold a team of horses to E. G. Paddock, which were afterwards reclaimed. The capture of these two ends the career of about all the horse-rustlers in this country.
articles.summary: Horse-thieves known as the "Two Jacks" captured at Mitchell.

articles.text: To look at Fred Willard one would not think him such a guileless youth. Attempting to cross Sully creek lately he found it was swimming and then turned carefully up the bank so as not to discourage any future comers from attempting to cross by seeing where the horse had turned around. His Honor Cole coming along behind and thinking where man had crossed before, there he could cross, plunged boldly in. That is the reason Cole is wearing a clean shirt.
articles.summary: Joke: Fred Willard's tracks lead Judge Cole into swimming Sully creek.

articles.text:
Frank Frisby, Bismarck, Dak. — "Drugs, Paints and Oils"; correspondence solicited
G. D. Kennedy, Medora, Dak. — "Cedar Posts for Sale": good cedar posts delivered in Medora and on the cars if required, at $15 per hundred
King jeweler, Spearfish or Deadwood — "Freighters Attention!" watch repairs
A. T. Packard, Medora, Dakota — "For Sale": six cows, twelve two-year-old steers, ninety two and three-year-old heifers, nine yearling heifers and two bulls, stock from Minnesota and Iowa; horses and outfit with cattle if desired
articles.summary: Small notices in column 2: drugs, cedar posts, watch repairs, and Packard's own cattle for sale.

articles.text: The St. Paul jobbers passed through Medora on their way east, Tuesday evening.
articles.summary: St. Paul jobbers pass through Medora.

articles.text: Col McClellan leaves to-night for Valley City and Moorhead. He intends farming near the latter place.
articles.summary: Col. McClellan leaving to farm near Moorhead.

articles.text: Howard Eaton reports that there is a good Indian down the river. His friends are requested to come and bury him.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton reports a dead Indian down the river.

articles.text: A force of men are here repairing the drip pans on the refrigerator cars. They were so low that the water slopped out of them to the floor of the car.
articles.summary: Men repair drip pans on the refrigerator cars.

articles.text: The session of court for this district begins at Mandan next Tuesday, August 11. There are one hundred civil and thirty-five criminal cases on the docket.
articles.summary: District court opens at Mandan August 11.

articles.text: Mr. L. C. Magee and wife and F. M. Magee, all of Pittsburgh, arrived Monday night for a visit to the Eaton's. They have gone to the logging camp and before they leave will visit the VI ranch.
articles.summary: Pittsburgh Magees visit the Eatons.

articles.text: Frank Axthelm, who has been running Fred Banan's barber shop for the last two months will leave next Tuesday. Banan, having completed his service in the army, will return to take permanent possession of his shop.
articles.summary: Fred Banan returning from the army to his barber shop.

articles.text: Howard Eaton and a companion killed an elk last week on Magpie creek, the first one that has been killed near here for some time. It was a fine fat cow elk and the VI outfit have been picking fat from their teeth ever since.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton kills an elk on Magpie creek.

articles.text: Tommy Smith came in Monday from the E6 ranch. He reports that there will be about 4,000 steers shipped from this range during the next month or two. Messrs. Clark & Plum have between 50,000 and 75,000 cattle in the Indian Territory and will probably drive a large number of these to their E6 ranch next year.
articles.summary: E6 ranch expects to ship about 4,000 steers.

articles.text: Attention is called to the change in the N. P. time-table, which went into effect last Sunday. West bound express freight No. 13, has been changed to 8:59 p. m., instead of 5:00 a. m. Eastbound passenger No. 2, now arrives at 8:36 a. m., a change of seven minutes and east bound freight No. 16 arrives at 1:50 a. m. instead of 1:45 p. m.
articles.summary: Northern Pacific time-table changes.

articles.text: The round-up which has been working the country between the bend of the Little Missouri and the railroad and the Big Missouri and the Bad Lands, finished its work last week. The outfits represented were the Hashknife, VI, 777, OX, SOHO, Maltese cross, Elkhorn and others. The whole country was thoroughly worked, but the only animals found were nine belonging to the OX outfit.
articles.summary: Round-up north of the railroad finishes; Maltese Cross and Elkhorn among outfits.

articles.text: E. G. Paddock returned Monday night from his Black Hills trip, accompanied by Mrs. Fred Willard and baby and John Ryan, of Spearfish. All the creeks, especially at this end of the line were swimming and some of them were only crossed with great difficulty. The abundant rains had caused millions of mosquitos to appear, making the trip extremely disagreeable. Mrs. Willard and baby stood the trip remarkably well.
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock returns from the Black Hills with passengers over flooded creeks.

articles.text: A cow-boy named James Boyd was killed about two weeks ago on O'Fallon creek. He was working for the "Capital B" outfit, whose ranch is on the Sandstone. When last seen alive, he had just turned over a bunch of cattle to a brother cow-boy. The horse he was on was not very bridle-wise and it is supposed that he fell over a bluff with Boyd into O'Fallon creek. The body was found about three days after the fatal accident. Boyd was a first-class cow-boy and all who knew him, deeply mourn his loss as he seemed to have no enemies whatever.
articles.summary: Cowboy James Boyd of the Capital B outfit killed in a fall on O'Fallon creek.
